source.title: Fisher information and the geometry of memorization in neural networks
source.authors: Daniel T. Bernstein; Chase Goddard; L. di Carlo; Wave Ngampruetikorn; David J. Schwab

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: Tests memorization under 10% label corruption, a related but narrower setting than the claim’s full random-label and noise-fraction assertions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work on fitting arbitrary labels and learning shared structure before noisy samples; those cited findings are not this study’s results. Its own label-noise experiment trains a ResNet-20 on 10% randomly corrupted labels and reports training, test, and corrupted-sample accuracy.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own SGD-trained ResNet-20 fitting results in two narrower settings: CIFAR-10 augmented with Gaussian images and CIFAR-10 with 10% corrupted labels. These bear on V3 and V4 even though neither experiment tests every part of those versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: Fisher geometry can separate memorized and generalizing information in these settings, depending on layer and Fisher evaluation data; suitable projections can also partially recover generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10 with 10% randomly corrupted labels, then studies Fisher-based weight projection; it does not train on completely random labels as in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Layer and the dataset used to compute the Fisher change the projection results.

fits_no_version.finding: Fisher projections selectively reduce memorization, with separation depending on layer and Fisher evaluation data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-training Fisher projections can separate memorized information from generalizing information under particular layer and data choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Transformer held-out regression-task performance improves early and subsequently worsens as training tasks are memorized.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small transformers trained on a finite set of latent regression tasks can exhibit transient in-context generalization before task overfitting.

fits_no_version.finding: The barcode linear model predicts risk reductions from deleting uninformative features and an interior-optimal projection rank at higher flip rates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-fit feature projection in a finite-sample linear model can trade off noise removal against loss of predictive signal.

record.problems: The label-noise experiment uses only one corruption fraction, so it cannot establish a smooth trend across fractions. The supplied text does not state the number of ResNet-20 models for the main label-noise results.
record.rows_left_out: No rows retained: the relevant label-noise results report one 10% corruption condition, which does not establish the fraction sweep required by V4; the other versions are not tested.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling of the entire training set, chance test performance, and fitting without architecture or hyperparameter changes relative to true-label training.
Relative training time for true and random labels, and convergence speed across corruption fractions. The reported 200 epochs and 1–2 GPU hours provide no such comparison.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and training on an entirely unstructured dataset. Gaussian images constitute only 500 added examples alongside structured CIFAR-10 data.
Perfect fitting across a corruption-fraction sweep and steadily increasing test error toward chance. Only 10% label corruption is tested in the deep-network experiment.
Comparisons establishing whether explicit regularization prevents fully random-label fitting, and whether removing regularization harms true-label generalization.
Training-time ordering of learning real-label patterns versus noisy or random labels. Fisher projection results concern trained models; the transformer dynamics concern latent-task overfitting.

missing.what: Add baseline fitting results for the Gaussian experiment: 500 synthetic Gaussian images added to CIFAR-10, independently assigned labels, and 100% training accuracy including 100% Gaussian-set accuracy. Table 2 reports 84.3% CIFAR-10 test accuracy at k=0.
missing.locator: Section 3; Appendix A.1; Tables 1 and 2, Gaussian model, k=0.

missing.what: Restore the explicitly omitted 10% label-noise baseline as result rows: 100% training accuracy, 100% accuracy on corrupted samples under assigned labels, and 73.4% CIFAR-10 test accuracy. The stated omission is unjustified: a single fraction bears on V4's fitting-and-retained-signal component without establishing its trend.
missing.locator: Section 3; Tables 1 and 2, noisy-label model, k=0.

record.verdict_notes: No existing rows require correction because the record contains none. Missing entries identify results needed to ground the text-based verdicts, including the label-noise results already declared omitted. The record's E2 combines values from different models: 73.4% is the noisy-label baseline, whereas 83.9, 83.7, 83.4 and 83.1 are projected Gaussian-model test accuracies. Neither a partial dataset condition nor an untested corruption sweep warrants a limits_scope verdict.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labeling, chance-level test error under that condition, and whether fitting required changes to the original architecture or training hyperparameters.
Training-time comparison with true labels and convergence across corruption fractions.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs trained to zero training error.
The study tests only 10% label corruption; it does not report a sweep from no corruption to fully random labels or a steady test-error trend across corruption fractions.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent fitting random labels, and whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels in the claimed sense; the paper cites this as prior work and studies a different task.
